For example A7. Required for a form sheet — without a date there is no telling which day the figures belong to.
Without this cell the whole sheet is skipped. Use it for a cell whose absence makes the rest meaningless.

A difference within this band is logged as "matching". 0 means every difference, however small, is reported.

Leave it empty and every run has to choose a plant. Fill it in when the template serves only one plant.
Dry run done and the log looks right? This run writes for real into the weather, performance and metering stage records.
Line "%s" declares a range of several cells, so the target has to be a measurement point — a single field cannot take thirteen values.
the file says %(a)s, the system computes %(b)s — a difference of %(c).3f%%. This is where our formula and the plant's have not yet met.
%(a)s lies in the future (today is %(b)s). Almost always a wrong date cell, or the time zone of the machine that produced the file.
Form sheet: a cell address, for example B20. For an hourly range, declare a single-row range such as D40:P40 — with the Value range field beside it.
Leave it empty to read EVERY sheet in the file. Real reports arrive weekly with one sheet per day, so leaving it empty is the right thing.
Form-sheet template "%s" does not declare the cell holding the report date. Without a date, none of the figures read can be placed anywhere.
A daily operations report is a FORM SHEET: it cannot be read by column, because the column holding the figure changes from row to row. A file exported from SCADA is a TABLE.
Line "%s" has a factor of 0 — every value read becomes 0 with nothing to report an error. Use 1 when no unit conversion is needed.
Line "%(n)s": the timestamp range has %(a)d cells, the value range has %(b)d. With different counts there is no telling which value belongs to which hour.
Refused by default: re-importing the same day has to be deliberate rather than accidental. Tick this when the plant sends a corrected report.
An import template tells the system which cell in the file goes into\n which field. Declared once, after which each day is just an upload.
Some cross-check lines DIFFER: the figure the plant computed is not the figure the system computes. The file's figure is still written as-is; the difference is in the log.
Only used when Cell/range is a RANGE of timestamps. For example D41:P41. The two ranges have to hold the same number of cells, otherwise there is no telling which value belongs to which hour.
Copy the label as it appears in the source file, for example "Energy Output (Inverter)". It is not used for lookup — it is there so whoever reads the log can match it against the sheet in their hand.
The stage code in the metering chain, for example INV, MCB, EVN. Looked up by CODE rather than by internal key, so the same template works for every plant that follows the same code convention.
the sheet name says %(a)s while cell %(o)s says %(b)s. Usually a sheet copied without correcting the date cell — writing by the cell would overwrite the older day's data. The whole sheet is skipped.

a NEGATIVE loss of %(l).1f kWh: this stage (%(a).1f) is higher than the one before it (%(b).1f). Energy does not increase on the way through a stage — check the unit factor, or whether two cells have been swapped.

Multiply the raw value by this. If the report is in MWh while our table stores kWh, the factor is 1000. Without it, 255 MWh becomes 255 kWh — a thousandth, while the figure stays positive and looks plausible.

Timestamps in a file almost never carry a time zone, while Odoo stores UTC. Reading local time as UTC shifts the whole curve by 7 hours — the chart still looks smooth, with the irradiance peak at 5 in the morning.
Choose an import template, upload the file, press Dry run. A dry\n run does everything a real import does and then rolls it back, so the\n log shows the outcome in advance with nothing written.

An operator copying yesterday's sheet and forgetting to correct the date cell is something that really happens, and the consequence is overwriting the older day's data. A sheet name carrying the date can be cross-checked; where they disagree it STOPS, because writing the wrong day is worse than not writing.

Line "%(n)s" writes into a metering stage, which always means the energy field, so no field can be chosen. Choosing a field only means something with "cross-check only" on — for example checking the loss %% the plant computed against the loss the system computes.

One line per pair, "value in the file = value in the system", for a selection field. For example:
Sunny = sunny
Sunny/Cloudy = partly
Cloudy = cloudy
A value missing from the table is SKIPPED with a line in the log, rather than guessed at.

Only used for the Metering stage target. The same report has rows from SCADA (inverter energy) and rows from a meter (energy received at the grid substation). Record them under one label and later nobody knows which figure has an invoice behind it.

Odoo's one2many does NOT copy by default. Left at the default, duplicating a template — the most natural way to make one for a second plant — produces an empty template, and it is empty silently: the screen opens looking perfectly normal.

Read it, compare it with the figure the system computes itself, and record the difference in the log — do NOT write it into the data. The report carries the plant's own results (PR, denominator, temperature factor), so every import is an occasion on which our formula is checked against their own figures.

These are the results of a dry run: every write was performed and then rolled back, so the log below is exactly what a real import would do — the cross-check included. Nothing has reached the database.

In a form sheet, the column holding the figure changes from row to row, because the merged regions of long and short labels differ. In a real report the weather block has its values in column P while the loss block just below has them in column O. So every line has to declare the exact cell; do not assume "the value is always in the column to the right".
Point at the middle of a merged region and Excel returns empty with nothing to say so — the import log will tell you which cell actually holds the value.

Factor — the report is in MWh while our table stores kWh, so the factor is 1000. Without it, 255 MWh becomes 255 kWh: a thousandth, while the figure stays positive and looks plausible.
Cross-check only — a line carrying the plant's own results (PR, denominator, temperature factor). Read it, compare it with the system's figure, record the difference in the log, do not write it into the data. Every import is an occasion on which our formula is checked against their own figures.
